result.summary: After Paris dies, the Trojans fight on outside their walls, and slaughter spreads on both sides. Apollo rouses Aeneas and Eurymachus, Neoptolemus rallies the Greeks, and Aphrodite finally removes Aeneas. The next day the Greeks assault the walls in a shield-roof formation, but Aeneas, strengthened by a god, hurls them back.

scenes.title: Slaughter before Troy's walls
scenes.summary: Trojans and Greeks kill one another in a long catalogue of deaths while Strife, Enyo and the Fates look on.
scenes.stakes: Both armies risk death in battle, and Troy risks its fall.

scenes.title: Apollo rouses the Trojans
scenes.summary: Apollo, disguised as Polymestor, inspires Aeneas and Eurymachus, and the Greeks flee until Neoptolemus rallies them. Zeus clears the dust, Pallas turns the tide, and Aphrodite carries Aeneas off.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk rout, and Aeneas risks death at Pallas' hands.

scenes.title: Retreat and tending the wounded
scenes.summary: The Trojans retreat behind their walls, and both camps tend their wounded and dead.
scenes.stakes: The survivors face wounds and mourning.

scenes.title: Assault on the walls
scenes.summary: The Greeks attack each gate; Aeneas smashes their shield-roof with stones, kills Alcimedon, and trades taunts with Philoctetes.
scenes.stakes: Troy risks capture, and the attackers risk being crushed.

analysis.text: Fate rules over gods and men alike, and the poem repeatedly shows Troy's doom as fixed whatever anyone does.
The poem imitates Homeric battle scenes with catalogues of deaths and long similes, as an epic of the later Roman imperial era.

fun_facts.text: The Fall of Troy is by Quintus of Smyrna, who wrote in Greek about the 3rd century AD, and it continues the Iliad.

language_notes.text: The Erinyes (Furies) were goddesses of vengeance who pursued wrongdoers; here they serve as a frightening comparison for Strife and Enyo.
"Besprent" is archaic for sprinkled or spattered.
Leto, pregnant by Zeus and pursued by Hera, bore Apollo and Artemis; the poet says Lycia's Xanthus river was revealed during her labour.
"Love's nursing-debt" means the duty of a grown child to repay parents for rearing him, which Hippasus never lived to do.
The rock of the Fire-god (Hephaestus) refers to a place in Lycia where natural flames burned continually, the Chimaera fire.
The syntax is compressed: the archer aims the arrow at the arch of the bow's horn, ready to shoot as Menoetes rushes him.
"The fates on the arrow riding" means death itself travels with the arrow; the heart is called the seat of thought and strength.
Far-darter is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god; the disguised Polymestor is said to be the son of a seer and of his priest.
Fate spinning 'destiny-threads' pictures the Fates as spinners; the god means long lives lie ahead for these two.
Enyo is a goddess of war, often paired with Ares, who delights in the screaming din of battle.
A partizan is a long-bladed spear or halberd. 'Shore though' means sheared through.
The hind is the farm laborer driving the oxen; he fears the plough may cut their hamstrings.
Myrmidons were the soldiers once led by Achilles, now following his son.
Cronion means son of Cronos, a name for Zeus (here Jove's Greek counterpart).
'Nor recked of Zeus' means Fate paid no heed even to Zeus; here Fate stands above the gods.
"Bedabbled" and "besprent" are archaic: smeared or splashed. The women take the warriors' blood-stained armour from them.
"Leeches" here means physicians or healers, from an old word for doctor.
"Gates that fated the plain" is obscure; it seems to mean gates facing the plain, toward the Greek ships.
A twibill is a double-bladed axe or mattock, used here to hack at the walls and gates.
Refers to Zeus' war with the Giants, when Atlas, who held up the sky, was shaken by the turmoil.
"Played the men" is an old idiom meaning they fought bravely, behaving like true men.
Cytherea is Venus, Aeneas' divine mother; she is said to have turned the arrow aside. "Poeas' son" is Philoctetes.

context_notes.text: Enyo is a goddess of war and Strife is Eris; both accompany armies and spur the killing.
The Sangarius is a river of Phrygia in Asia Minor, near Troy's region.
Philoctetes inherited the bow of Heracles, whose arrows were deadly; he killed Paris with it earlier in the poem.
Syme is a small island near Rhodes; Nireus led its contingent to Troy.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, who has come to Troy after his father's death and fights with Achilles' fierce spirit.
Aeneas was the son of Aphrodite, so Thetis, Achilles' mother, steers her grandson away from him out of respect for the goddess.
Pallas is Athena, who favored the Greeks and helped plan Troy's destruction.
Aphrodite mourns Paris, who was killed earlier in the war; Aeneas is destined to survive Troy's fall.
Ocean was thought a great river encircling the world; Dawn's horses rising from it is the poet's way of saying morning came.
Capaneus' son is Sthenelus, Diomedes' companion; the Scaean gate was Troy's main western gate.
Aeneas, son of Venus and Anchises, was a leading Trojan; here a god strengthens him.
The Locrians were the troops of Aias (the lesser Ajax), who leads them in this assault.

literary_notes.text: Panic-fear, Dread, Ares and the Fates act as figures moving among the armies, giving the battle a supernatural presence.
The severed head with parted lips, as if to shriek, makes the death grotesquely vivid.
The fishermen's skill at sea cannot save them in battle, a bitter reversal of their craft.
The twitching severed arm is compared to a snake's cut tail, stressing its pointless, mindless movement.
Trojans scattering before the stone are likened to cranes scattered by a farmer's sling, showing their panic.
Falling warriors are compared to trees torn down by a storm, with sound echoing the earth's thunder.
The Trojans' sudden fury is compared to wasps attacking bees, an extended image of rage and swarming speed.
Falling ranks are likened to grain cut by reapers, making slaughter seem like orderly, relentless labor.
Strife is made a figure who gloats over the dead, showing war's spirit enjoying the carnage.
Fleeing Greeks become raiding swine chased by dogs, a deflating image; Phoebus is the pleased farmer.
The severed hand still gripping the reins is a grim, uncanny image that heightens the terror.
The Trojans driven back are compared to waves hurled back by a counter-wind, conveying the shifting tide of battle.
Fate is a pitiless spinner whose thread decides the lives of men and cities, setting a theme of inevitability.
The fallen warriors are compared to timbers scattered on a beach when a ship is dismantled, turning slaughter into a vivid image of wreckage.
The locked shields are likened to a solid roof that wind and rain cannot pierce, conveying the formation's strength.
The advancing Greeks are compared to a long dark winter cloud trailed across the sky, suggesting a slow, ominous mass.
The murmuring of the army is compared to bees humming around hives, giving the sound a living, busy quality.
Aeneas' stone is likened to a thunderbolt, and the collapse of a cliff onto goats shows the Greeks' terror.
Alcimedon sees Troy for the first and last time as he reaches the parapet, a grim irony of a triumph that ends in death.
Medon's fall is compared to a wild goat shot by a hunter dropping from a crag, making the death vivid.
Philoctetes' taunt that Aeneas fights like a woman from a tower shows his pride in archery and his scorn.
